summary: Maps Extensible Provisioning Protocol statuses to those in the Registration Data Access Protocol, and registers new RDAP statuses where needed so all EPP statuses are covered.

eli5.summary: Domain registries use one set of labels behind the scenes and show another to the public. This matches them up so none is missing.

subtitle: A lookup table that makes sure every domain registry status in EPP has a matching label in RDAP.

tldr.problem: Domain registries that use EPP track objects with many status values, but the RDAP registry of statuses had no matching value for a number of them. Data could not be shown accurately in RDAP.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists each EPP status next to its RDAP status, finds the blanks, and registers new RDAP status values built by turning the camelCase EPP name into lowercase words with spaces.
tldr.outcome: Every EPP status named in the cited RFCs now has an RDAP status, and the client versus server distinction on prohibited actions is preserved.

facts.label: Mapping rule
facts.value: Each EPP status maps to a single RDAP status

facts.label: Naming rule
facts.value: camelCase to lowercase words with spaces

today: RFC 8056 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The new status values it describes were registered by IANA in the "RDAP JSON Values" registry.

sections.title: Why a Status Mapping Is Needed
sections.content:
Domain name registries often run the Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP) to manage registered objects. Anyone looking up that data through the Registration Data Access Protocol (RDAP) sees statuses taken from the "RDAP JSON Values" registry, which RFC 7483 describes.

RFC 8056 maps the statuses defined in the EPP RFCs to the statuses in that RDAP registry. The EPP sources are the domain, host and contact mappings (RFC 5731, RFC 5732, RFC 5733) and the grace period mapping (RFC 3915).

The rule it sets is that each EPP status MUST map to a single RDAP status, so registry data can be presented accurately in RDAP.
sections.eli5: Two groups use different words for the same things. This paper says which word on one side matches which word on the other.

sections.title: The Statuses That Already Match
sections.content:
The RFC writes the mapping as EPP status = RDAP status, leaving the right side blank where RDAP has no equivalent. A handful of EPP statuses already have a counterpart.

Some differ only in spelling: ok maps to active, and linked maps to associated. The pending family maps directly to pending create, pending delete, pending renew, pending transfer and pending update. The status inactive maps to inactive.
sections.eli5: A few words already had a twin on the other side, like two names for the same toy.

sections.title: Gaps and the Naming Rule
sections.content:
Most of the remaining EPP statuses had a blank on the RDAP side. That includes the grace periods (addPeriod, autoRenewPeriod, renewPeriod, transferPeriod, redemptionPeriod), pendingRestore, the hold statuses and all the prohibited statuses.

The RDAP registry already had general values such as renew prohibited, update prohibited, transfer prohibited and delete prohibited, but they do not map directly to the EPP ones. EPP can tell apart an action blocked by server policy from one blocked at a client's request, and that ability needs to be preserved in RDAP.

The fix is a simple naming rule. The new RDAP value is the EPP value converted from camelCase to lowercase, with a space inserted at each word boundary. So clientHold becomes client hold.
sections.eli5: When a word was missing, they made a new one by splitting the long word into small lowercase words, like turning "bigRedBall" into "big red ball".

sections.title: Client and Server Prohibited Statuses
sections.content:
The new prohibited values come in client and server pairs. A client value means the client asked for the restriction. A server value means the server set it.

  • client delete prohibited and server delete prohibited: requests to delete the object MUST be rejected.
  • client renew prohibited and server renew prohibited: requests to renew MUST be rejected.
  • client transfer prohibited and server transfer prohibited: requests to transfer MUST be rejected.
  • client update prohibited and server update prohibited: requests to update, other than to remove this status, MUST be rejected.
  • client hold and server hold: DNS delegation information MUST NOT be published for the object.
sections.eli5: Some locks are put on by the owner and some by the building manager. The new labels tell you who put each lock on.

sections.title: Grace Periods and Restore Statuses
sections.content:
Four of the new values are grace periods during which a client that deletes the object gets a credit from the server for the cost of the action that started the period.

  • add period: after the initial registration; credit for the registration.
  • auto renew period: after a registration period expires and the server extends it automatically; credit for the auto renewal.
  • renew period: after the client explicitly renews; credit for the renewal.
  • transfer period: after a successful transfer of sponsorship from one client to another; credit for the transfer.

Two more cover deletion. redemption period means a delete was received, but the object is not yet purged because it can still be restored, which aborts the deletion. pending restore means the object is being restored after being in the redemption period.
sections.eli5: A grace period is like a return window at a shop: for a while after you buy something, you can give it back and get your money back.

sections.title: What IANA Registered
sections.content:
IANA added each new value to the "RDAP JSON Values" registry with Type: status. Every entry carries a description matching the one in the RFC and a pointer to the EPP status it maps to, such as the domain mapping in RFC 5731 or the grace period mapping in RFC 3915.

For every entry the registrant name is the IESG, with contact iesg@ietf.org. The final mapping, with all new values in place, covers each EPP status in the list.
sections.eli5: The official keeper of lists wrote each new label into the master list, with a note saying which old label it matches.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The status values can be subject to server-side information disclosure policies that restrict showing them to authorized clients. Implementers may wish to review RFC 7481 for the RDAP security services that can be used to implement those policies.
sections.eli5: Some labels may only be shown to people who are allowed to see them, like a staff-only notice board.
